items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “an indentation at the base of a cliff between high and low tide levels, cut by erosion”.
items.answer: Wave-cut notch
items.markingKey: Wave-cut notch: an indentation at the base of a cliff between high and low tide levels, cut by erosion. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of a wave-cut platform.
items.answer: Waves erode a notch at the cliff base between high and low tide by hydraulic action and abrasion; the overhang collapses; repetition causes the cliff to retreat, leaving a gently sloping platform; debris is removed and abrades the platform.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: Explain how geology influences the formation of headlands and bays.
items.answer: On discordant coasts less resistant rocks (clays, sands) erode faster to form bays, more resistant rocks (chalk, limestone, granite) remain as headlands; joints and faults are lines of weakness.

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a cross-section of the wave-cut platform at Kimmeridge Bay, Dorset. The platform is 280 m wide from the cliff foot to the low-water mark and falls 4.6 m over this distance. The cliff is retreating at about 0.12 m per year. Calculate how long the platform would take to form at the present rate of retreat.
items.answer: about 2 333 years

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a cross-section of the wave-cut platform at Robin Hood’s Bay, Yorkshire. The platform is 276 m wide from the cliff foot to the low-water mark and falls 6.7 m over this distance. The cliff is retreating at about 0.53 m per year. (a) Calculate how long the platform would take to form at the present rate of retreat. (b) Suggest why the platform may be older than your calculated value.
items.answer: (a) about 521 years (b) Retreat may have been slower in the past, sea level has changed since the last glacial, and part of the platform may have formed during earlier high sea levels.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that geology is more important than wave energy in explaining the formation of cliffs and headlands.
items.answer: For: Lithology and structure (joints, faults, dip) control resistance and profile; discordant coasts form headlands and bays (Swanage, Dorset). Against: Wave energy, fetch and refraction control erosion rates; sub-aerial processes and sea-level change shape profiles; time also matters. Conclusion: Geology controls where landforms develop and their form, but waves supply the energy, so both are essential.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a gently sloping rocky surface left at the foot of a retreating cliff”.
items.answer: Wave-cut (shore) platform
items.markingKey: Wave-cut (shore) platform: a gently sloping rocky surface left at the foot of a retreating cliff. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Bays are always formed in softer rock.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They may also form along faults or joints in a single rock type.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how rock structure influences cliff profiles.
items.answer: Dip of strata: seaward-dipping beds give sloping cliffs prone to slides; landward dip gives steep cliffs; joints and faults allow erosion; alternating hard and soft beds give stepped profiles.

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a cross-section of the wave-cut platform at Robin Hood’s Bay, Yorkshire. The platform is 372 m wide from the cliff foot to the low-water mark and falls 6.1 m over this distance. The cliff is retreating at about 0.15 m per year. Calculate the mean gradient of the platform as a ratio and as an angle.

Fig. 6.1 is a cross-section of the wave-cut platform at the Kaikoura Peninsula, New Zealand. The platform is 397 m wide from the cliff foot to the low-water mark and falls 3.1 m over this distance. The cliff is retreating at about 0.45 m per year. (a) Calculate how long the platform would take to form at the present rate of retreat. (b) Explain why the rate of cliff retreat slows as the platform widens.
items.answer: (a) about 882 years (b) Waves break further out and lose energy crossing the platform, so less energy reaches the cliff foot.

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a cross-section of the wave-cut platform at Robin Hood’s Bay, Yorkshire. The platform is 209 m wide from the cliff foot to the low-water mark and falls 3.1 m over this distance. The cliff is retreating at about 0.4 m per year. (a) Calculate the mean gradient of the platform as a ratio and as an angle. (b) Suggest why the platform may be older than your calculated value.
items.answer: (a) 1 in 67; 0.8° (b) Retreat may have been slower in the past, sea level has changed since the last glacial, and part of the platform may have formed during earlier high sea levels.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end, formed by longshore drift where the coast changes direction”.
items.answer: Spit
items.markingKey: Spit: a long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end, formed by longshore drift where the coast changes direction. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of a spit.
items.answer: Longshore drift carries sediment along the coast; where the coast changes direction, deposition continues out into the sea in sheltered, deeper water; wind and waves curve the end (recurved tip); a salt marsh forms behind.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.stem: Explain the development of a sand dune system.
items.answer: Sand dries and is blown landward; it is trapped by obstacles and pioneer plants; embryo dunes grow into yellow dunes stabilised by marram grass; humus accumulates to form grey dunes; dune slacks and climax heath or woodland further inland.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [4]

items.answer: (a) 1 in 29; 2° (b) Waves break further out and lose energy crossing the platform, so less energy reaches the cliff foot.

items.stem: Assess the view that the supply of sediment is the most important factor in the formation of depositional coastal landforms.
items.answer: For: Without sediment from cliffs, rivers and offshore, spits, bars and dunes cannot form; dams and defences that cut supply cause erosion (e.g. the Nile delta). Against: Wave energy and direction, longshore drift, coastal shape, tides, wind for dunes, vegetation and sea-level change also control formation. Conclusion: Sediment supply is a necessary condition, but the form and location of features depend on processes and coastal configuration.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “spit”?
options: A ridge of sediment that extends across a bay or river mouth, enclosing a lagoon.
A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end, formed by longshore drift where the coast changes direction.
A ridge of sediment that joins an island to the mainland.
A ridge of sand or shingle at the top of a beach formed at the limit of the swash of constructive waves.
items.answer: A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end, formed by longshore drift where the coast changes direction.
items.markingKey: Spit: a long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle attached to the land at one end, formed by longshore drift where the coast changes direction. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Beach sediment usually becomes finer in the direction of longshore drift.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Attrition reduces particle size along the drift direction.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a tombolo.
items.answer: Wave refraction around an island creates a zone of low energy behind it; longshore drift or swash-aligned deposition builds a ridge linking the island to the mainland.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a drowned river valley formed when sea level rises, with a winding outline and decreasing depth inland”.
items.answer: Ria
items.markingKey: Ria: a drowned river valley formed when sea level rises, with a winding outline and decreasing depth inland. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of a ria.
items.answer: River valleys were cut when sea level was lower during glacials; the post-glacial (Flandrian) eustatic rise drowned the lower valleys, producing winding inlets with tributary arms that become shallower inland.

items.stem: Compare the characteristics of rias and fjords.
items.answer: Rias: drowned river valleys, V-shaped cross-section, gentle sides, deepest at the mouth. Fjords: drowned glacial troughs, U-shaped, steep sides, very deep with a shallow threshold at the mouth, straighter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per comparison [4]

items.stem: A raised beach at northern Norway lies 24 m above present sea level. Shells in the beach are dated to about 7 thousand years ago, when global (eustatic) sea level was about 7 m lower than today. Calculate the mean rate of uplift in millimetres per year.
items.answer: 4.4 mm per year

items.stem: A raised beach at northern Norway lies 29 m above present sea level. Shells in the beach are dated to about 9 thousand years ago, when global (eustatic) sea level was about 21 m lower than today. (a) Explain why the land has risen. (b) Describe the landforms associated with the raised beach.
items.answer: (a) The weight of the ice sheet depressed the crust during the last glacial; after the ice melted, the land has slowly rebounded (glacio-isostatic adjustment). (b) A flat terrace of beach deposits backed by a relict cliff, sometimes with caves, arches and stacks now inland and vegetated.

items.stem: Assess the view that isostatic change has had a greater impact than eustatic change on coastal landforms. In your answer you may refer to raised beaches and rias.
items.answer: For: In formerly glaciated regions (Scotland, Scandinavia, Canada) rebound produced raised beaches and relict cliffs; isostatic subsidence drowns other coasts. Against: The post-glacial eustatic rise of about 120 m drowned river valleys and glacial troughs worldwide, forming rias, fjords, estuaries and barrier islands, and set the level of present-day processes. Conclusion: Eustatic change has had the more widespread effect, but isostatic change dominates locally in formerly glaciated regions.

items.stem: A student writes: “All raised beaches were formed by a fall in global sea level.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many, as in Scotland, result from isostatic uplift of the land.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a raised beach.
items.answer: Beaches and cliffs formed at a former sea level; isostatic uplift after deglaciation (or a fall in sea level) left them above present sea level, where they are no longer affected by waves.

items.stem: A raised beach at the Gulf of Bothnia, Sweden lies 15 m above present sea level. Shells in the beach are dated to about 9 thousand years ago, when global (eustatic) sea level was about 19 m lower than today. Explain why the coast may now be affected by both emergence and submergence.
items.answer: Isostatic uplift is slowing while eustatic rise from thermal expansion and ice melt is accelerating, so in some areas relative sea level now rises.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Spits form only where there is a large tidal range.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They need a supply of sediment, longshore drift and a change in coastline direction; strong tidal currents can limit their growth.

items.answer: Correct. They absorb wave energy and store sand that replenishes beaches during storms.

items.stem: “The supply of sediment is the most important factor in the formation of depositional coastal landforms.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Without sediment from cliffs, rivers and offshore, spits, bars and dunes cannot form; dams and defences that cut supply cause erosion (e.g. the Nile delta). Against: Wave energy and direction, longshore drift, coastal shape, tides, wind for dunes, vegetation and sea-level change also control formation. Conclusion: Sediment supply is a necessary condition, but the form and location of features depend on processes and coastal configuration.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “ria”?
options: A drowned river valley formed when sea level rises, with a winding outline and decreasing depth inland.
A former beach left above present sea level when the land rose or sea level fell.
A drowned glacial trough with steep sides, great depth and a shallow threshold at its mouth.
An old cliff, now inland and above the reach of the sea, behind a raised beach.
items.answer: A drowned river valley formed when sea level rises, with a winding outline and decreasing depth inland.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Fjords were eroded by rivers and then drowned.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They were eroded by glaciers below sea level and then flooded.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision website states: “A coastline can show evidence of both emergence and submergence.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Compare the characteristics of rias and fjords.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Eustatic and isostatic changes have alternated, as in Scotland. (b) Rias: drowned river valleys, V-shaped cross-section, gentle sides, deepest at the mouth. Fjords: drowned glacial troughs, U-shaped, steep sides, very deep with a shallow threshold at the mouth, straighter.

items.stem: A raised beach at the Isle of Jura, Scotland lies 9 m above present sea level. Shells in the beach are dated to about 9 thousand years ago, when global (eustatic) sea level was about 20 m lower than today. Explain why the coast may now be affected by both emergence and submergence.
items.answer: Isostatic uplift is slowing while eustatic rise from thermal expansion and ice melt is accelerating, so in some areas relative sea level now rises.

items.stem: “Isostatic change has had a greater impact than eustatic change on coastal landforms.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to present sea-level rise and fjords.
items.answer: For: In formerly glaciated regions (Scotland, Scandinavia, Canada) rebound produced raised beaches and relict cliffs; isostatic subsidence drowns other coasts. Against: The post-glacial eustatic rise of about 120 m drowned river valleys and glacial troughs worldwide, forming rias, fjords, estuaries and barrier islands, and set the level of present-day processes. Conclusion: Eustatic change has had the more widespread effect, but isostatic change dominates locally in formerly glaciated regions.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the formation of a wave-cut platform. (b) A revision website states: “Wave-cut platforms can widen indefinitely.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Waves erode a notch at the cliff base between high and low tide by hydraulic action and abrasion; the overhang collapses; repetition causes the cliff to retreat, leaving a gently sloping platform; debris is removed and abrades the platform. (b) Not correct. As they widen, waves lose energy before reaching the cliff, slowing erosion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per stage [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the formation of a wave-cut platform. (b) Explain how rock structure influences cliff profiles.
items.answer: (a) Waves erode a notch at the cliff base between high and low tide by hydraulic action and abrasion; the overhang collapses; repetition causes the cliff to retreat, leaving a gently sloping platform; debris is removed and abrades the platform. (b) Dip of strata: seaward-dipping beds give sloping cliffs prone to slides; landward dip gives steep cliffs; joints and faults allow erosion; alternating hard and soft beds give stepped profiles.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per stage [4] (b) [3]

items.stem: Fig. 6.1 is a cross-section of the wave-cut platform at Robin Hood’s Bay, Yorkshire. The platform is 342 m wide from the cliff foot to the low-water mark and falls 5.4 m over this distance. The cliff is retreating at about 0.2 m per year. Suggest why the platform may be older than your calculated value.
items.answer: Retreat may have been slower in the past, sea level has changed since the last glacial, and part of the platform may have formed during earlier high sea levels.

items.stem: Assess the view that geology is more important than wave energy in explaining the formation of cliffs and headlands.
items.answer: For: Lithology and structure (joints, faults, dip) control resistance and profile; discordant coasts form headlands and bays (Swanage, Dorset). Against: Wave energy, fetch and refraction control erosion rates; sub-aerial processes and sea-level change shape profiles; time also matters. Conclusion: Geology controls where landforms develop and their form, but waves supply the energy, so both are essential.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the formation of a ria. (b) Explain the formation of a raised beach.
items.answer: (a) River valleys were cut when sea level was lower during glacials; the post-glacial (Flandrian) eustatic rise drowned the lower valleys, producing winding inlets with tributary arms that become shallower inland. (b) Beaches and cliffs formed at a former sea level; isostatic uplift after deglaciation (or a fall in sea level) left them above present sea level, where they are no longer affected by waves.
